title: Show HN: KradleBench – Multi-agent AI evals in Minecraft
author: jamest
snippet: Hi HN - This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you! Our team shipped a benchmark…
excerpt: Hi HN - This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you! Our team shipped a benchmark: KradleBench. We test AI in Minecraft Worlds. 1. The worlds are multi-agent. Humans and other AIs are in there too, often pursuing their own goals. Collaboration and conflict skills fall out of this property. 2. The world are dynamic. They constantly change, which means that agents need to react. “Capture the Flag” has a single winning condition, and many different ways to achieve it. This leads to many emergent and creative strategies. 3. The worlds are real-time. They are not turn-based, they do not wait for AIs to finish thinking. Nature balanced speed and intelligence in humans, we can understand this in AIs too. Underneath all this is Kradle, a platform to test and understand intelligence. It’s a petri dish where any intelligence type (LLM, World Model, Human) can be compared and generate useful information to improve current systems, whether it’s on capabilities or safety. Some findings so far: - A skilled human was #1, until yesterday when Astra 6.2 surpassed them. We lose badly on solo tasks and out-compete on multi-agent ones - Astra 6.2 iterates on its strategy 4x faster than Fable 5.2. The Claude family tends to think hard and stick with strategies. The OpenAI models tend to be more reactive and iterative, which serves them well in multi-agent, dynamic, real-time evals. We’ve got videos on all the top model’s page, and we’ll be producing them when a new model launches. Sign up on the site to get them and for when the platform opens. Thanks for reading, James & Kemal

title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
snippet: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation Overview AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes…
excerpt: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation Overview AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. This guide covers four things: - Three eras of evaluation (section 1). Evaluations moved from checking answers, to checking what an agent did, to checking what a team of agents produces. Each step adds software that can change the score. - The steps in an agentic evaluation (section 2). We follow one task through eight steps, from the claim to the reported score.
